messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammad, a 27-year-old Middle Eastern male and physical therapist, experienced a traumatic sexual assault while he was walking home from work one night. The event had left him with deep emotional scars and a profound sense of vulnerability that permeated his daily life. The trauma was set off by a specific scent—a cologne worn by the perpetrator—and this olfactory trigger has since become acutely potent in Mohammad’s environment. Whenever he catches a whiff of similar scents, it feels as though the assault is happening again. The smell evokes a visceral reaction that plunges him back into the fear and helplessness he felt on that night. In addition to the scent triggers, physical pain also serves as a potent reminder. Any sensation in his body can quickly escalate into a full-blown panic attack. This somatic trigger has made it difficult for Mohammad to engage in any form of physical activity or intimacy with his wife. He feels like he’s carrying a heavy burden that isolates him from the world and from her. Mohammad had come to believe that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, leading him to distance himself emotionally even from those close to him. The assault had left him feeling ashamed of his body and convinced that he couldn’t rely on himself in a crisis. These negative appraisals have significantly impacted how he perceives the world around him. The negative beliefs about himself have made Mohammad jumpy and easily startled, reacting with alarm at unexpected movements or touch from others. He often finds himself on high alert, constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger. This hyper-vigilance has extended to his work as a physical therapist, where he avoids touching patients and is particularly wary when they are in close proximity. Mohammad’s dissociative response—pretending the event happened to someone else—has only served to reinforce his negative appraisals and triggers. The more he dissociates, the less able he feels to trust himself or navigate the world without reliving the trauma. This maladaptive strategy has led him to avoid thinking about the assault altogether, which in turn amplifies his sensitivity to triggers. The cycle of fear and avoidance has tightened over time, making it increasingly difficult for Mohammad to function normally. His constant body monitoring and checking for signs of danger have become an exhausting routine that only heightens his startle response and feelings of vulnerability. His wife has noticed a significant change in him and is concerned about the distance he’s putting between them. The trauma has disrupted their intimate relationship, leaving both feeling isolated and hurt. Mohammad’s avoidance behaviors have also affected his work; he often finds himself distracted and unable to fully engage with patients. What finally brought Mohammad to seek help was a recent incident where he had a panic attack in front of his colleagues at the physical therapy clinic. He realized that if he didn’t address these issues, they would continue to erode every aspect of his life. The most frightening prospect for him is losing control and being unable to function as both a husband and a professional. Mohammad hopes that with help, he can reclaim some sense of normalcy and reconnect with the world around him without constantly feeling like danger lurks in every shadow and scent.
